Melania Trump und Papst Leo hatten vermittelt Ukraine bringt kurz vor Ende der lokalen Waffenruhe fast 200 Zivilisten aus Cherson in Sicherheit
Das ukrainische Militär hat kurz vor dem Auslaufen einer lokalen Waffenruhe 167 Menschen aus bedrohten Gebieten der südlichen Region Cherson evakuiert. Unter den Evakuierten seien 22 Kinder und 21 Menschen mit eingeschränkter Mobilität, teilte der ukrainische Generalstab am Sonntag mit. Die sechstägige Feuerpause in der russisch besetzten Stadt Oleschky und Umgebung sollte um Mitternacht Moskauer Zeit (21.00 Uhr MEZ) enden. Der Gouverneur der Region Cherson rief die Bewohnerinnen und Bewohner zur Wachsamkeit auf. Er warnte zudem eindringlich davor, Gebiete in der Nähe des Flusses Dnipro zu betreten, da die Intensität der russischen Angriffe dort hoch bleibe.
Die lokale Waffenruhe, die am Dienstag begann und von beiden Kriegsparteien eingehalten wurde, war nach Vermittlungsbemühungen von US-First Lady Melania Trump und unter Beteiligung von Papst Leo zustande gekommen. Es handelte sich um die längste lokale Unterbrechung der Kämpfe seit Beginn der russischen Großinvasion im Februar 2022.
Bereits am Samstag waren Bewohner aus Oleschky in die Ukraine gebracht worden. Sie reisten zunächst mit Bussen über die von Russland bereits 2014 annektierte Halbinsel Krim in die russische Stadt Anapa und flogen von dort nach Belarus, von wo aus sie in die Ukraine weiterreisten. Der Sprecher des Präsidialamtes in Moskau sagte russischen Nachrichtenagenturen zufolge, man bewerte den Ablauf des Einsatzes in Oleschky sowie die Koordination zwischen den Menschenrechtsbeauftragten beider Länder positiv.
- 
2 Min
Russische Streitkräfte hatten die Stadt am Fluss Dnipro unmittelbar nach der Invasion im Februar 2022 unter ihre Kontrolle gebracht. Ukrainische Truppen eroberten jedoch noch im selben Jahr einen großen Teil der Region zurück, einschließlich der Gebietshauptstadt Cherson. In anderen Teilen der Ukraine gingen die Kämpfe am Sonntag weiter. Regionale Behörden meldeten mindestens zwei Todesopfer bei Angriffen in der Region Sumy an der russischen Grenze und in der zentralukrainischen Region Winnyzja.

A113.text:
EU- und Nato-Land Russlandfreundliche Präsidentin Jotowa liegt bei Stichwahl in Bulgarien vorn
Bei der Stichwahl um das Präsidentenamt liegt das amtierende Staatsoberhaupt Iliana Jotowa ersten Prognosen zufolge vorn:
- Zwei Nachwahlbefragungen, die nach Schließung der Wahllokale am Sonntagabend veröffentlicht wurden, ergaben für Jotowa rund 51 Prozent.
- Ihr Konkurrent, der frühere Interimsregierungschef Andrej Gjurow, kam auf 43 bis 45 Prozent.
Die 61-jährige Jotowa gehört dem Lager des als russlandfreundlich geltenden Regierungschefs Rumen Radew an. Gjurow hingegen wird von prowestlichen und reformorientierten Parteien unterstützt. Im ersten Wahlgang vor einer Woche mit 27 Kandidaten hatte Jotowa zwar die meisten Stimmen erhalten, die absolute Mehrheit bei einer historisch niedrigen Wahlbeteiligung jedoch verfehlt. Mit einem offiziellen Ergebnis der Stichwahl wird am Montag gerechnet.
Laut den Nachwahlbefragungen lag die Wahlbeteiligung nun bei etwa 27 bis 29 Prozent und damit etwas höher als bei der ersten Runde am 25. Oktober, bei der die Wahlbeteiligung mit 23 Prozent einen historischen Tiefstand erreicht hatte.
- 
1 Min
Die Wahl zu dem weitgehend repräsentativen Amt findet vor dem Hintergrund von Drohnenangriffen vor der bulgarischen Küste statt. Dort waren in den vergangenen Wochen Behördenangaben zufolge mindestens sechs Handelsschiffe von Drohnen attackiert worden. Dies schürte Sorgen in dem EU- und Nato-Land vor einer Ausweitung des Ukrainekriegs. Die Ukraine macht Russland für die Angriffe verantwortlich. Auch Radew erklärte, die Attacken schienen für Russland von Vorteil zu sein. Moskau wies eine Verantwortung jedoch zurück. Jotowa und Gjurow verurteilten die Angriffe und forderten ein diplomatisches Ende des Krieges.
Sollte Jotowa die Wahl gewinnen, wäre sie die erste direkt gewählte Präsidentin Bulgariens. Sie hatte das Amt im Januar kommissarisch übernommen, nachdem Radew zurückgetreten war, um bei der Parlamentswahl im April anzutreten, die er mit einem russlandfreundlichen Programm gewann. Radew lehnt militärische Unterstützung für die Ukraine ab und warb für bessere Beziehungen zu Moskau sowie die Wiederaufnahme russischer Öl- und Erdgaslieferungen. Er sicherte aber nach seiner Wahl eine proeuropäische Politik zu. Der 50-jährige Gjurow, der in diesem Jahr als Übergangsministerpräsident amtierte, gilt als Unterstützer der Ukraine und hatte während seiner Amtszeit ein Sicherheitsabkommen mit der Regierung in Kyjiw unterzeichnet. Auch mehrere konservative und rechtsgerichtete Politiker wie Ex-Ministerpräsident Bojko Borissow sprachen sich für Gjurow aus.

A119.text:
Laut Uno Mehr als 300.000 Männer, Frauen und Kinder sind im Jemen auf der Flucht
Im Westjemen sind mehr als 300.000 Menschen auf der Flucht, wie die Vereinten Nationen berichten. Der Grund: die wieder aufgeflammten Kämpfe zwischen der proiranischen Huthi-Miliz und von Saudi-Arabien unterstützten Regierungstruppen.
Nahezu alle Betroffenen seien in den vergangenen zwei Monaten aus ihren Heimatorten geflohen, erklärte die Internationale Organisation für Migration (IOM) am Sonntag. Die Menschen bräuchten »dringend Schutz, Nahrung, sauberes Wasser und Gesundheitsversorgung«.
Nach vier Jahren relativer Ruhe hat sich der Konflikt zwischen den Huthis und den Regierungstruppen im Jemen seit Juli wieder intensiviert. Im September starteten die Huthis eine neue Offensive im Westen des Landes. Saudi-Arabien, das die international anerkannte Regierung im Jemen unterstützt, griff seither mehrfach Huthi-Stellungen an.
- 
1 Min
Die Lage für die Menschen in der von den Huthis belagerten Stadt Taizz ist offenbar besonders dramatisch.
Es herrsche ein akuter Mangel an Treibstoff, Lebensmitteln, Wasser, Medikamenten und Kochgas, teilte die Menschenrechtsorganisation Human Rights Watch (HRW) mit. »Die Huthis können die humanitäre Katastrophe, die sie bei der Zivilbevölkerung verursachen, nicht mit der Belagerung von Taizz rechtfertigen«, sagte Niku Dschafarnia, Jemen-Expertin bei HRW. Die Huthis müssten unverzüglich die Einfuhr von Lebensmitteln, Treibstoff, Medikamenten und Wasser sowie die Lieferung humanitärer Hilfe ermöglichen, um weiteres Leid zu verhindern.
Die Huthis belagern die Großstadt nach Angaben von Anwohnern der Stadt inzwischen vollständig. Taizz war bereits ab 2015 jahrelang von den Huthis belagert worden. Nachdem 2024 einige Zufahrtsstraßen geöffnet worden waren, ist sie im Zuge einer neuen Offensive erneut eingekesselt.
Preis für Wasser verdreifacht
Die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) warnt in einem jüngsten Bericht vor Ausbrüchen übertragbarer Krankheiten. Die Provinz Taizz gehört laut WHO zu den am stärksten betroffenen Gebieten eines Choleraausbruchs in dem Bürgerkriegsland. Zugleich beherberge sie mit rund 126.000 Menschen den größten Anteil der Vertriebenen im Jemen. Die Lage in Unterkünften, bei der Wasserversorgung und in sanitären Einrichtungen stellt weiterhin die größten Gesundheitsrisiken dar. Zudem gebe es Unterbrechungen bei der Abfallentsorgung.
Das Uno-Nothilfebüro Ocha blickt besonders besorgt auf die Wasserversorgung in Taizz. Viele Menschen in der Stadt seien auf Trinkwasser aus Lastwagen angewiesen, sagte Ocha-Sprecher Jens Laerke kürzlich. Der Diesel werde jedoch knapp. Die Wasserproduktion habe sich innerhalb der vergangenen Wochen halbiert und der Preis für das gelieferte Wasser verdreifacht, erklärte der Sprecher weiter. Einige medizinische Hilfsgüter hätten Taizz laut WHO erreicht, aber weitere müssten aufgrund eingeschränkter Zufahrtswege in Lagern in Aden liegen bleiben.

A14.text:
UN staffer’s death in custody exposes Houthi ‘political extortion’ in Yemen
The United Nations and human rights experts demand an independent investigation after an arbitrarily detained staff member died in Houthi custody in Yemen.
The United Nations is demanding a thorough investigation into the death of a human rights employee while in Houthi detention in Yemen.
Mohammad el-Shami, who worked for the UN Human Rights Office, died more than a month ago but his family was only recently notified. He had been arbitrarily detained by the rebel group, which controls much of northern Yemen, since June 2024.
His death has highlighted the number of UN and NGO workers targeted by the Houthis, since they captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has urged the Houthi authorities in Sanaa to ensure a prompt, transparent and independent investigation into el-Shami’s death.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the UN Human Rights Office and the wider United Nations. Mohammad’s family has not received any explanation of the cause or circumstances of his death – they deserve to know the truth,” said Turk.
“This requires disclosure of all relevant medical and detention records, preservation of evidence and independent scrutiny of any stated cause of death. There must be accountability for wrongdoing.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed his dismay and demanded the immediate release of all detained personnel.
“I am appalled & deeply saddened by the death of a @UN colleague, Mohammad el Shami, while in the custody of the Houthi de facto authorities in Yemen,” Guterres stated.
“I remain gravely concerned for the safety & wellbeing of the UN personnel, former UN staff & personnel from humanitarian & civil society organisations who remain detained. I reiterate my call for their immediate & unconditional release.”
The Houthis have repeatedly accused detained workers of being spies.
The Houthis accused more than 60 UN and NGO workers detained in 2024, when el-Shami was arrested, of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.
The group has routinely arrested civil rights activists, NGO workers and other civilians on espionage allegations.
As of February this year, 73 UN staff and dozens of other humanitarian workers were in detention, according to Amnesty International. El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi custody, following the death of a World Food Programme employee in February 2025.
The Minister of Human Rights for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Meshdal Mohammed, held the militia fully responsible for el-Shami’s abduction, forced disappearance and death.
“The continued abduction of [civil rights workers] for more than two years, culminating in the announcement of the death of one of them without enabling his family to visit him or know his condition, dictates a serious review of the way this file is handled,” he said.
Local human rights advocates highlight the severe difficulty of achieving accountability for deaths and other civil rights abuses by the Houthis.
Tawfik Alhamidi, President of SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, outlined the systematic obstacles faced by NGO workers operating in Houthi-controlled territories in Yemen.
“The group is the one that controls prisons, medical records and witnesses, in addition to the fact that there is no judicial or human rights oversight over places of detention,” he told Al Jazeera.
“This delay by this group and the withholding of information may reflect a systematic pattern or behaviour by this group, at least in order perhaps to hide some features or make it difficult to conduct an examination.”
He said that the deaths of many Yemenis in Houthi custody have been put down to disease, sudden death or suicide.
The Houthi authorities remain fully accountable for any deaths in custody, regardless of the exact cause, Alhamidi added.

UN’s peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in the disputed Western Sahara region came to an end Sunday after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate. Morocco, which claims the region as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents from the Algeria-backed Polisario Front called it "unacceptable".
The UN's long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a US-Russia standoff at UN headquarters over the territory’s future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa’s northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
“This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period,” Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the UN secretary general, said in a statement. “A smaller team reporting to the United Nations’ Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the UN Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft US resolution that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.

Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force’s mandate.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute".
The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision". The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the "excessive bias'' of the US draft resolution.
The UN classifies Western Sahara as a “non-self-governing territory”, while critics of Morocco’s control describe it as Africa’s last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the “free zone” that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.
After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.

Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco’s foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco’s diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.
The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.
A UN-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.
The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized.

A2.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts a missile as fighting rages in Yemen’s al-Jawf
Houthi-affiliated media report that seven people were wounded in strikes on the city of Hodeidah.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says air defences intercepted a Houthi missile, while fighting continues to rage along key fronts between the armed group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile” targeting Saudi Arabia’s southern region, said coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki in a statement on Monday.
Earlier, he said defences destroyed a drone launched toward the southern region on Sunday evening.
Also on Monday, the Saudi Civil Defence authority issued and then lifted alerts warning of “potential danger” in the city of Abha, as well as the provinces of Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran.
The authority warned residents against “filming, publishing or sharing information” related to missile and drone attacks.
In Yemen, a media outlet affiliated with the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), reported that seven people were wounded in Saudi-led coalition air strikes on Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast.
Four people were wounded in the attacks on Ras Isa port dock, while three others suffered injuries in a strike on an oil company site in the governorate’s Bajil district, Houthi media reported.
There was no comment on the reports from the Saudi-led coalition.
Humanitarian crisis
The latest clashes come as Yemeni government forces keep up their campaign to regain positions from the Iran-aligned Houthis in the strategic northern governorate of al-Jawf.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Sunday evening that government forces conducted 1,272 “targeting operations” against Houthi fighters, fortifications and weapons supplies over 24 hours.
Operations are ongoing in al-Jawf, neighbouring Marib and al-Bayda to the south, added al-Nazili. Government forces killed roughly 500 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled nearly 170 vehicles, equipment or heavy weaponry.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
In southwest Yemen, the Houthis continue to besiege the city of Taiz, blocking the entry of food, fuel and medical supplies, in what authorities warn is a mounting humanitarian crisis.
Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan has called for urgent help for the city’s deteriorating health facilities. He said 120 health centres have stopped operating and another 66 are close to shutting down since the Houthis cut off supply routes to the city in early October.
Nour al-Din al-Mansouri, a member of the committee facilitating the work of the Taiz Siege Affairs Office, told Al Jazeera that at least 23 trucks were damaged or overturned in the past two weeks while seeking alternative routes to Taiz.
The city is Yemen’s third-largest and home to about one million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
Full-scale fighting reignited in Yemen in September, when the Houthis made crucial gains that tightened their grip on the Red Sea coast.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a campaign called Operation Dawn of Yemen last month to regain Houthi-held sites and restore government control over other territories held by the group, which seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.

A28.text:
Saudi civil defence sounds all-clear after alerts in southern cities
Nov 2 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia's civil defence authority on Monday said the threat had passed shortly after issuing alerts for the southern and western cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, Taif and Najran, amid weeks of escalating hostilities with Yemen's Houthis.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen later said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-aligned Houthis towards the southern region of Saudi Arabia.
Southern Saudi Arabia, which borders Yemen, has come under repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting military installations and energy infrastructure, including Jazan, home to a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery on the Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia has also carried out airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, as the renewed fighting heightens risks to the kingdom's oil production and exports.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and oil export facilities in Yanbu, a key Red Sea outlet for Saudi crude shipments.

A32.text:
Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes
Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to "take care" of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
In the most intense phase of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks across the region. Iran-aligned armed groups joined the fighting in Lebanon and Yemen.
Akraminia's remarks followed Trump's suggestion that the United States could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.
"We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Trump reiterated his threat on Sunday, telling a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of midterm elections, that he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
The warning came after US media reported that Trump had held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday over whether and when to ramp up combat operations against the Islamic republic.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with Iran, with Netanyahu pressing the president to strike the country immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as "tough", while the US source said it was "direct", according to Axios.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump confirmed he had discussed Iran with Netanyahu, but would not elaborate.
- 'No geographical limitations' -
Top military and political officials in Iran have warned against any new attack.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday echoed a warning issued a day earlier in a written message by Iran's new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
"In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy," Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: "We hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy," adding that Iran "remains prepared for both defence and diplomacy", according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in "tone" from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, "neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations".
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran, Qatari mediators hold third day of talks to end US-Iran war
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the November 3 US midterm elections. President Donald Trump has said the United States will not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action afterwards.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared for "both defence and diplomacy".
Speaking to state media, Araqchi said discussions on a "two-day proposal" were continuing, but that no final conclusion had been reached.
Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Araqchi as saying in an interview on Saturday that Iranian and Qatari negotiators had developed a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of a potential agreement with Washington.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East.
"We are doing our best in this process, and we hope that there is rationality on the other side so that they prioritise diplomacy over other paths," Araqchi said of the talks with Qatari officials.
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday ordered the armed forces to be prepared for any attack, while the military later announced steps to strengthen its readiness.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday for discussions with Iranian officials before moving the talks to Doha on Saturday, an official had told Reuters. The talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington, the official added.
(Reporting by Andrew Mills and Elwely Elwelly; Writing by Nayera Abdallah, Editing by Joe Bavier and Ros Russell)

A41.text:
Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
- Published
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with the fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.
"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.
- AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened 
  - Published22 October
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

A423.text:
Temperature soars at Swedish grocery store freezers, one store blames hackers
STOCKHOLM, Nov 2 - The temperature of freezers at several Swedish grocery stores rose sharply overnight, operators ICA and Coop said on Monday, with at least one store blaming the incident on a cyberattack.
French police last month said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a large-scale attack, causing food losses and fires, and underlining the vulnerabilities of connected systems.
One Swedish store on Monday said on social media that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 F), similar to the attack in France.
"We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems," a spokesperson at privately held ICA said in an email.
Privately held grocery retail group Coop told daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.
Coop did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

A425.text:
Belgian government crisis looms as budget talks collapse
BRUSSELS, Nov 2 - Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever was set to hand in his resignation on Monday, following late-night coalition talks that failed to reach a compromise on budget cuts, Belgian media reported.
De Wever arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels on Monday morning for a meeting with Belgian King Philippe.
He was widely expected to offer his resignation, after his five-party coalition again failed to agree on next year's budget.
De Wever's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the prime minister did not speak to the press as he arrived at the palace.
The government has been arguing for months over €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in budget cuts and tax increases De Wever says are needed to keep state finances in check.
The crisis coincides with heightened stress on financial markets, where interest rates have risen sharply on government bonds of Belgium, France and other European countries seen to have weak government finances.
Belgium's king was not expected to immediately accept the resignation of De Wever's government, newspaper De Tijd cited sources as saying, but could instead send De Wever back for a last push at the negotiating table.
If De Wever's resignation is accepted, the king could ask other parties to form a new coalition, or it could lead to new elections.
De Wever has repeatedly warned of an "interest snowball" without budget cuts, where Belgium would need to take on new loans to be able to pay interest on existing debt.
In months of talks, De Wever's Flemish nationalist N-VA and the liberal MR have not been able to compromise with their socialist and centrist coalition partners.
The N-VA and MR have pushed for cuts in spending including on healthcare, while their partners demand higher wealth taxes to bring in more resources. REUTERS

A44.text:
France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

A50.text:
Peaceful protests in Germany spiral into violence and looting
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
The rallies were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge". Thousands had taken part in the largely peaceful demonstrations across Germany before violence broke out.
At least 54 people were arrested in Frankfurt and over 100 police officers left injured, according to German authorities.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were outbreaks of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
This comes as protests have been taking place across Europe over the rising cost of living, poor public services, and a lack of affordable housing.
The BBC's world correspondent Joe Inwood reports.

A58.text:

German ministers pledge tough action after rioters damage stores in Frankfurt
Demonstrators took to city streets in Germany to demand better education and lower living costs
German ministers threatened tough penalties for looters and rioters who damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in Frankfurt overnight, while still praising public forces for preventing larger-scale violence.
Frankfurt became the hot spot for violent protests late on Saturday, after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of dozens of German cities during the day to demand better education and lower living costs in protests led by the campaign group "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z takes charge").
In Frankfurt's financial hub, hooded rioters damaged 17 shops and stores, of which five were looted, Roman Poseck, interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Sunday.
He said police deployed 1,300 officers, with more than 100 injured in clashes. Police arrested 54 people aged between 13 and 29.
"I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this," Poseck said.
Poseck said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of a migrant background, citing information from the police.
"Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background."
Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances including windows being smashed and petrol bombs being thrown at the emergency services.
"The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild tabloid on Sunday
"This breach of the peace must be followed by tough penalties."
He accused "violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community" of hijacking the otherwise peaceful protests, without elaborating.
Dobrindt said the police strategy of maintaining a large presence while deploying officers across multiple locations had worked.
"Excesses of violence like those in Paris were prevented thanks to our highly committed police forces," Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said.
In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses.

A69.text:
Pese a la caída de la movilización y una menor conflictividad en las protestas de este sábado, el tercero consecutivo a nivel nacional, Francia encara una nueva semana de tensión social por la probable vuelta de los bloqueos en la educación y una huelga general el jueves.
El Gobierno francés, bajo presión después de las imágenes de caos de la protesta del 17 de octubre, celebró que las últimas manifestaciones se desarrollaron en calma, a pesar de la "violencia inaudita" de algunos alborotadores, en palabras del ministro de Interior, Laurent Nuñez.
Causaron especial conmoción en el país las imágenes del lanzamiento de un artefacto incendiario contra gendarmes en París, lo que provocó que un agente se prendiera en llamas, si bien solo sufrió heridas leves. El ministro Nuñez calificó ese ataque de "tentativa de homicidio" en declaraciones a la prensa por la noche.
En total, durante la jornada, se registraron cuatro policías y un gendarme heridos en todo el país.
El férreo dispositivo policial y las restricciones a la circulación también lograron evitar grandes incidentes durante la noche, que se temía problemática por los llamamientos -por parte de grupúsculos de ultraizquierda y otros colectivos radicalizados- en redes sociales a aprovechar la noche de Halloween para cometer actos de violencia.
Al final, la jornada se saldó con 565 arrestos (según el balance oficial hasta las 21 horas), una cifra significativamente menor que los 1.314 del sábado de la semana pasada y los 2.628 del 17 de octubre.
También cayó la movilización en las manifestaciones en general, ya que, según el Gobierno, hubo 320.000 personas en las calles, frente a las 550.000 de la semana pasada.
Huelga y nuevos bloqueos educativos
Frente a esa aparente desactivación de la movilización, el Ejecutivo galo encara las próximas jornadas de con "humildad" y "vigilancia" según indicaron este domingo al canal BFMTV fuentes gubernamentales, que también reconocieron que el 17 de octubre hubo un "fallo de anticipación" que se tradujo en una grave crisis del orden público.
Y es que el comienzo de noviembre supone la vuelta a las aulas tras un parón de 15 días por las vacaciones de otoño y, con ello, nuevos llamamientos del movimiento estudiantil a retomar los bloqueos en los centros de secundaria y universitarios.
Fueron esas acciones, en protesta por el deterioro del sistema de educación público, las que desde finales de septiembre pusieron la semilla de la gran movilización que se dio en Francia en las últimas semanas, a medida que se iban sumando otras causas de protesta, como el descontento por la pérdida de poder adquisitivo.
Las principales organizaciones de estudiantes llaman a retomar los bloqueos desde el martes y a sumarse el jueves a la convocatoria de huelga general que los sindicatos franceses han lanzado para el 5 de octubre, en la que también participarán otros colectivos, como los empleados ferroviarios.
"No se han atendido nuestras reivindicaciones", afirmó este domingo, en declaraciones a la cadena pública Franceinfo, Sabrine Kharbach, portavoz de Union étudiante.
Algunas agrupaciones estudiantiles, sin embargo, piden realizar bloqueos ya desde este lunes, como la organización Les Lycéens.
Los estudiantes piden invertir 10.000 millones de euros para solventar los problemas de la educación pública y ven insuficientes las medidas anunciadas hasta ahora por el Gobierno.
Acusan al Ejecutivo de Emmanuel Macron, además, de buscar desactivar el movimiento creando "desorganización" y "caos", en particular con la imposición de restricciones a las manifestaciones (como ocurrió ayer, cuando no pudieron discurrir por el centro de las ciudades).
Entre las promesas realizadas ya por el Gobierno figuran limitar el número de alumnos por clase, contrataciones adicionales de docentes y modificar ya en este curso Parcoursup, la denostada plataforma de admisión a la enseñanza superior.

Morocco, which claims the Western Sahara as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.
The Polisario Front has been seeking an independent state in Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain left in 1976.
A peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place there since a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991.
November 1 would mark the start of the “liquidation phase” of the mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement.
The end of the peacekeeping mission comes a year after the UN Security Council adopted a US-drafted resolution that accepted Rabat's plan to give the territory autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the "most feasible" solution to the conflict.
Russia, which abstained in last year's vote, this year vetoed another US-backed resolution that would have cemented the UN's preference for the Moroccan plan while scaling back the peacekeeping force.
The Security Council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
Besides monitoring the ceasefire, MINURSO was tasked with organizing a referendum that has never taken place due to disagreements over voter eligibility.
Morocco's Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita told state media that the mission's reference to a referendum - the “R” in its name - was an "anachronism".
Rabat had been informed that Russia was going to block the US-drafted resolution, but saw it as "an opportunity to review certain rules of the game", he said.
Morocco's royal palace had said the non-renewal of the mission was a "significant development" towards withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council.
Algeria's Foreign Ministry on Saturday expressed "deep regret" over the non-renewal, blaming the "excessive bias" of the US towards Morocco's position.

A87.text:
By Shubham Kalia and Kanjyik Ghosh
Binance said withdrawals were stabilizing after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial". The exchange said it had now covered 95% of the $6.3 billion of stolen assets.
The heist, which analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust the exchange with their money after the attack. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited as of 1530 GMT. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $4.36 billion.
"This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted)," a spokesperson for Binance said of the DefiLlama data.
Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in phases, prioritising user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin.
"We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand," Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.
Binance said earlier on Sunday that it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may take longer to source in the required amounts, it said.
FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT
The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.
Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.
Analysts had also pointed to North Korea's involvement. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
US President Donald Trump, however, later on Saturday said it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved.
"We don't know if it's North Korea — but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters in comments posted by a White House account on X.
BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTS
Binance has been working with other crypto firms to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located as of Friday, it said.
The exchange has repeatedly said it will bear the financial impact of the hack and has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses.
The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance's $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.
Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that Binance would use 50% of its SAFU funds, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 billion.
Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe.
[truncated]

A89.text:
A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo. The ceasefire was due to expire at midnight Moscow time (2100 GMT).
It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
"Units of civil-military cooperation of the 'South' group of forces, in cooperation with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region," Ukraine's General Staff wrote on Telegram.
It said the evacuees included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared.
"I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called 'red zones' – areas and settlements near the Dnipro," Prokudin wrote on Telegram. "The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries' human rights commissioners.
The pope said he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
Melania Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire "has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack".
On Saturday, starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine after a circuitous journey from the area, just a few km (miles) from the front line.
They first travelled by bus via Crimea, annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine.
Those wishing to leave Oleshky - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys.
It was not known how many chose to stay in Russian-held Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River opposite the region's Ukrainian-held main town of Kherson.
CEASEFIRE HOLDING
The ceasefire has been holding since Tuesday without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town.
Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year.
Military action continued in other parts of Ukraine on Sunday.
Regional governors and emergency services reported one death in a strike in the Sumy region on the Russian border, a frequent target, and at least one in the central region of Vinnytsia.
(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Alessandra Prentice; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

A118.text:
Ilijana Jotowa vs. Andrej Gjurow Mehr Moskau oder Europa? Stichwahl entscheidet über Bulgariens Kurs
Vor dem Hintergrund mehrerer Drohnenangriffe auf Handelsschiffe im Schwarzen Meer wählt Bulgarien am Sonntag in einer Stichwahl sein neues Staatsoberhaupt. Die russlandfreundliche Amtsinhaberin Ilijana Jotowa tritt dabei gegen den prowestlichen Herausforderer Andrej Gjurow an. Die Abstimmung gilt als Entscheidung über den künftigen außenpolitischen Kurs Bulgariens – vor allem mit Blick auf den Ukrainekrieg und das Verhältnis zu Moskau.
Jotowa sagte nach ihrer Stimmabgabe in der Hauptstadt Sofia, sie wolle »ein starkes Bulgarien in einem starken Europa«, das »souverän in seinen Entscheidungen« sei. Sie unterstützt die EU- und Nato-Mitgliedschaft ihres Landes, lehnt Militärhilfen für die Ukraine aber ab. Im Wahlkampf inszenierte sie sich als »Präsidentin des Friedens«, die mit Moskau in einen Dialog treten will.
Stichwahl um das Präsidentenamt in Bulgarien, Aufnahme vom 1. November 2026: Wohin steuert das Land?
Foto: Valentina Petrova / AP / dpa
Ihr 50-jähriger Herausforderer Gjurow sagte nach seiner Stimmabgabe in Blagoewgrad, er habe für ein »sicheres, stabiles und europäisches Bulgarien« votiert. In einer TV-Debatte vor der Stichwahl hatte er Jotowa vorgeworfen, dass sie Russland nicht ausdrücklich für die Angriffe auf Schiffe im Schwarzen Meer verantwortlich gemacht habe.
Überraschung im ersten Wahlgang
Anfang und Mitte Oktober waren vor der bulgarischen Schwarzmeerküste vier Handelsschiffe von Drohnen getroffen worden. 21 Menschen werden seitdem vermisst, sie sind vermutlich tot. Regierungschef Rumen Radew bestellte die russische Botschafterin ein, sah aber davon ab, offiziell einen Schuldigen zu benennen.
Im ersten Wahldurchgang vor einer Woche hatte Jotowa mit 35 Prozent der Stimmen nur knapp vor Gjurow gelegen, der auf 32 Prozent kam. Damit schnitt Jotowa deutlich schlechter ab als in Umfragen vorhergesagt. Die Wahlbeteiligung war in der ersten Runde mit lediglich 23 Prozent so niedrig wie noch nie gewesen. Bei der Stichwahl wurde eine höhere Beteiligung erwartet.
Bulgariens unabhängiger Präsidentschaftskandidat Andrej Gjurow
Foto: Valentina Petrova / Bulgarian News Agency / AP / dpa
Der Politikexperte Teodor Slawew bezeichnete den Ausgang der ersten Wahlrunde im Gespräch mit der Nachrichtenagentur AFP als »schallende Ohrfeige der Wähler für die Regierung Rumen Radew«, der sich wie Jotowa für einen Dialog mit Russland einsetze. Als einen der Gründe nannte der Experte »Jotowas wenig überzeugende Antwort auf die russischen Bedrohungen im Schwarzen Meer«.
Die 62-jährige Jotowa, eine ehemalige Journalistin und sozialistische Europaabgeordnete, hatte das Präsidentenamt erst im Januar von Radew übernommen. Dieser war zurückgetreten und hatte anschließend die Parlamentswahl gewonnen und das Amt des Ministerpräsidenten übernommen. Eine Bestätigung Jotowas als Staatschefin würde ihm Rückenwind verschaffen.
Streit über Waffenlieferungen für die Ukraine
Die Regierung hatte im Juni Waffenlieferungen aus Beständen der bulgarischen Armee an die Ukraine gestoppt und sich später aus der internationalen »Koalition der Willigen« zur Unterstützung Kyjiws zurückgezogen. Die bulgarische Rüstungsindustrie liefert allerdings weiterhin Waffen an Kyjiw.
Die Bulgaren sind in ihrer Haltung gegenüber Russland gespalten. Der Gründer des Umfrageinstituts Mjara, Parwan Simeonow, sagte, bei der Präsidentschaftswahl stünden sich zwei Visionen gegenüber: die eine »konservativ, populistisch und dem Osten zugewandt« und die andere »westlich, elitär und liberal«.
Im politischen System Bulgariens hat das Staatsoberhaupt vorwiegend repräsentative Aufgaben. Es kann allerdings ein Veto gegen Gesetze einlegen und ist Oberbefehlshaber der Streitkräfte des Nato-Mitgliedslandes. Jotowa wäre im Falle eines Siegs die erste gewählte Frau an der Spitze Bulgariens – im Januar hatte sie das Amt ohne Wahl übernommen.

A182.text:
Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion stolen from the platform last week.
The exchange moved to reassure crypto investors and said withdrawals were stabilizing after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial” after, what analysts believe, may be the world’s biggest financial robbery ever.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday. Ether hit a two-month low on Friday and also recovered a little to $2,287.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally. It said on Sunday it had $171 billion in total assets under management as of October 28.
The Binance theft adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust Binance with their money after the attack. The exchange said it had covered 95% of the assets stolen in the heist.
Explainer: Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded at Binance
Stablecoin market capitalisations tend to fall when money is leaving cryptocurrencies and they have dropped since Friday. The combined capitalisation of the two largest stablecoins, USDT and USDC, has dropped by about $1.2 billion since Friday, according to Coinmarketcap.com.
Spot bitcoin ETFs shed $643 million on Friday, the largest daily outflow of October, and more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.
“I get why, for conservative institutional investors, this is unsettling,” Redbord said.
“A hack at a financial institution means stolen usernames and passwords. A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital.”
Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using its money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may take longer to source, it said.
Despite those measures, some users were weighing options to hedge risks.
Jay Koh, vice president at the Asia Web3 AI Association, said he had not withdrawn any of his holdings from Binance, as most of his funds were held in a cold wallet, which was not impacted by the hack.
“I would not necessarily withdraw everything from Binance ... However, I do think it is prudent to review exposure, diversify custody arrangements and avoid keeping more assets on any single platform than necessary.”
Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in stages, prioritizing user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin.
“We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand,” Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.
It added, “Rest assured that market conditions are stable.”
Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited after the event.
Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $5.81 billion, up from the $4.36 billion it showed earlier. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updated figures.
“This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted),” a spokesperson for Binance said of the initial DefiLlama data.

A270.text:
AT A GLANCE
- Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators regarding a proposal to end the war with the United States, with a follow-up meeting possible.
- The discussions are based on a seven-step plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade, with Iran suggesting a faster implementation timeline.
- Iran's demands include the end of the US blockade and respect for its requirements, while concerns about potential conflict escalation remain amid the upcoming US midterm elections.
Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2.
The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.
The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries.
“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.
On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.
Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.
The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”
Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.
– Rappler.com

Kremlin says it assumes that the Ukrainian army used the Oleshky ceasefire to regroup in line with 'normal practice'

A424.text:
Ukraine says Russia used Oleshky ceasefire to reinforce positions
KYIV, Nov 2 - Ukraine's General Staff said on Monday that Russian forces had used a humanitarian ceasefire last week in the Russian-held southern town of Oleshky to strengthen their military positions.
The six—day ceasefire — brokered through US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo — was meant to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations from the frontline town. In total, nearly 800 people were evacuated, Melania Trump said on X.
However, Ukraine's General Staff said it had recorded rotations of Russian units, fortification of positions, expansion of anti—drone measures along roads, and increased logistics activity, including deliveries of ammunition.
"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.
"The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."
In a video address on Facebook, Ukraine's 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen" called on residents of the Kherson region not to ignore air raid sirens, saying that Russia had "used the ceasefire to prepare and strengthen its capabilities".
It said there were reasons to expect an intensification of hostilities.
The ceasefire, which took effect on October 27, expired at 2100 GMT on Sunday. It was the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full—scale invasion in 2022.
Yaroslav Shanko, head of the Kherson City Military Administration, said in a statement there had been a drone strike on Monday in the centre of the city, which lies on the west bank of the Dnipro River in Ukrainian-held territory, opposite Oleshky. No casualties were reported.
The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, said on Telegram that Russian forces had shelled and attacked with drones and aircraft 16 settlements in Ukrainian—controlled parts of the region, including its capital Kherson, in the 24 hours to 0400 GMT on Monday.
Ukraine's Ombudsman for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, writing on Telegram, said on Sunday that both sides had "upheld the obligations they undertook throughout the duration of this period." REUTERS

A427.text:
French school protests resume on smaller scale as students return from break
- French high school protests resumed on 2 November after a break, but only a few schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes saw blockade attempts.
- The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September and spread nationwide, then turned violent in October with clashes, riots and shop looting.
- Students want better schools, more teachers, more university places and fairer admissions; Minister Edouard Geffray offered €4 billion and 15,000 new places, but students said it was not enough.
AI generated
PARIS – French high school student protests resumed on Nov 2 on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as they returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported.
Hundreds of more than 3,000 high schools in France were blockaded in the weeks prior to the break. The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs in September, have spread across the country and broadened beyond education to focus on the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists and sometimes turning violent.
A wave of so-called “Gen Z” protests has swept across European countries, including Germany, Italy, Belgium and Albania, driven by grievances including the cost of living, the poor state of schools and perceived corruption.
In October, French protests degenerated into violent clashes with the police and outright riots in several cities, with shops looted, in a test for President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government.
“In terms of blockades – or rather, attempted blockades – the phenomenon is very marginal. We’re talking about just a handful of units, a few individual schools,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told radio station France Inter on the morning of Nov 2.
He said protests are allowed but preventing access to schools is illegal.
Police officers were present, TV footage showed, though not in full anti-riot gear.
Students want the renovation of ageing schools, more teachers, more university places and the end of a university admissions system they see as socially unfair.
Geffray offered last week to cap class sizes at 28, dedicate €4 billion (S$5.73 billion) to renovating schools, create 15,000 new places for students in higher education and a new admission system by 2028. High school student representatives said the offers were not enough and they would keep protesting. REUTERS

A428.text:

Nov 2 - Saudi Arabia's civil defence authority on Monday said the threat had passed shortly after issuing alerts for the southern and western cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, Taif and Najran, amid weeks of escalating hostilities with Yemen's Houthis.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen later said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-aligned Houthis towards the southern region of Saudi Arabia.
Southern Saudi Arabia, which borders Yemen, has come under repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting military installations and energy infrastructure, including Jazan, home to a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery on the Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia has also carried out airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, as the renewed fighting heightens risks to the kingdom's oil production and exports.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and oil export facilities in Yanbu, a key Red Sea outlet for Saudi crude shipments. REUTERS

Bulgaria's Iotova wins presidential runoff, near-final results show
Nov 2 - Bulgaria's acting President Iliana Iotova won the presidential runoff election, near-final results from the Central Election Commission showed on Monday, becoming the country's first elected female head of state amid low voter turnout.
With 99.95% of precinct protocols processed, the Iotova-Valchev ticket had won 57.58% of the vote, or about 1.1 million ballots, while opponents Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev received 39.47%, or about 749,500 votes.
About 2.95% of voters chose the "I support no one" option.
The runoff followed a first round on October 25 that gave no candidate the majority needed for an outright victory. Iotova and Valchev led with 34.6% of the vote, ahead of Gyurov and Kandev on 32%, advancing to Sunday's second round.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on a ticket many political analysts consider Kremlin-friendly.
Radev supports Iotova and they have both called for a diplomatic end to the Ukraine war. REUTERS

A434.text:
Saudi strikes on port, oil facility in Yemen wound seven: Houthis
- Saudi strikes hit Ras Issa port and an oil facility in Yemen’s Hodeidah province, wounding seven people, the Houthis said.
- The Houthis called the attacks a “flagrant violation” and said they damaged vital ports and civilian infrastructure used for food, aid and oil imports.
- The Saudi-led coalition said it carried out “a precision operation”, as Yemen’s fragile truce has collapsed and the UN says over 1,600 have died.
