SANAA – Yemen’s Houthis said on Nov 2 that Saudi strikes targeted a key Red Sea port and oil facility in Hodeidah province, wounding seven people.
The Iran-backed group is fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government after a civil war reignited in one of the world’s poorest countries.
Saudi-coalition strikes on Ras Issa port wounded four civilians, while three more were hurt in an attack on an oil facility in Bajil district, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X.
“These repeated attacks on oil facilities and vital ports constitute a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and add to the series of war crimes in Yemen that target civilians and critical infrastructure,” he said.
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah TV channel said earlier that Saudi Arabia had attacked a pier and commercial ship on Ras Issa port.
Hodeidah has the biggest seaport under Houthi control and is a key entry point for food and aid to areas they hold.
The Ras Issa port, north of the city, also serves to import and store oil.
Houthi media also reported strikes on Nov 1 targeting the faculty of medicine at Hodeidah University, in the same province, while two residents told AFP they heard an explosion in the area.
The Saudi-led coalition said it had conducted “a precision operation to neutralise vital resources” used by the Houthis.
A fragile 2022 truce in Yemen’s civil war fell apart in July after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting in Yemen reignited. AFP

A447.text:
Trump says US-Canada trade deal is close after talks with Carney
- Trump says a US-Canada trade deal is “very close” after talks with Carney, with both sides aiming for a “mutually beneficial” outcome in the coming weeks.
- The talks are more positive than the failed August negotiations, which broke down over tariffs, vehicle relief, and Canada’s concerns about French-language rules.
- Carney says Canada will protect its languages, culture and sovereignty, while also reducing reliance on the US by deepening trade ties with other partners.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said a US-Canada trade deal is “very close” after talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said both sides would work on a “mutually beneficial” outcome in the weeks ahead.
“We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada,” Trump told reporters, repeating his contention that the US has been “losing money for many years” in trade with its northern neighbor.
With Republican control of Congress at risk in US midterm elections on Nov 3, Trump and Carney offered the most upbeat outlook on trade talks since they collapsed acrimoniously in August.
Carney, in a social media post earlier on Nov 1, said he spoke with Trump, building on “recent constructive discussions” on the outlines of a deal that would create jobs, boost affordability for families and “fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty”.
“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Carney said.
Trump’s tariff policies have spurred Carney to reduce Canadian dependence on trade with the US. Last week, he hosted top European Union officials in Montreal as part of the effort to deepen ties with non-US trade partners.
After the EU meeting, Carney hinted in a Politico interview that the outcome of the US midterms would not have much of an impact to shift Trump’s policy stance. Canada will not rush into a trade agreement with the US if the terms are not in Canada’s best interest, he said.
“I spoke with the prime minister the other day,” Trump said on Nov 1, referring to Carney.
“I spoke to him again yesterday, and we have the concept of a deal that’s going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it will be fine for Canada.”
US-Canada trade talks collapsed in August when Carney’s envoy walked away from the deal, in part over a dispute about whether to extend proposed US tariff relief to medium and heavy-duty vehicles that Canada was seeking.
Canada also accused the US of seeking to curtail the use of French – one of Canada’s two official languages – such as regulations designed to promote French-language programming. The US has denied that was ever a key issue. BLOOMBERG

A448.text:
German ministers vow tough response to Frankfurt riots and looting
- German ministers promised tough penalties after Frankfurt riots and looting injured more than 100 police officers and damaged 17 stores, five of them looted.
- Hesse interior minister Roman Poseck said 1,300 officers were deployed and 54 people aged 13 to 29 were arrested after violent clashes.
- Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said perpetrators would be identified and held to account, and said the heavy police presence helped prevent wider violence.
AI generated
FRANKFURT/PEISSENBERG – German ministers threatened tough penalties for looters and rioters who damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in Frankfurt overnight, while praising security forces for preventing wider violence.
Frankfurt emerged as the main flashpoint on Oct 31 after tens of thousands of people rallied in dozens of German cities to demand better education and lower living costs in protests organised by the campaign group “Gen Z regelt” – “Gen Z takes charge”.
In the financial hub of Frankfurt, hooded rioters damaged 17 stores, five of which were looted, Roman Poseck, the interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Nov 1.
He said the police deployed 1,300 officers, and more than 100 were injured in clashes. The police arrested 54 people aged between 13 and 29.
“I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.
He said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of an immigrant background, citing information from the police.
“Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from an immigrant background,” he said.
Protesters throw petrol bombs at police
Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances, including windows being smashed and petrol bombs, rocks and bottles being thrown at emergency services.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said perpetrators would be identified and held to account.
“I expect there to be severe penalties. We are not prepared to accept, in the slightest, that such incidents and such rioting should take place here,” he told reporters on Nov 1.
He accused “troublemakers from the immigrant community” of acting alongside left-wing extremists and other far-left groups but did not provide evidence to support the claim or say which groups had joined the demonstrations.
Dobrindt said a policing strategy based on a large security presence and deployments across multiple locations had proved effective.
In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on Oct 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses.
Dobrindt said border controls had been tightened ahead of the protests out of fear that extremist groups from abroad could exploit them to stir riots. REUTERS

A450.text:
Houthis repeat threats against Saudi oil giant, aviation
- Houthis repeated threats against Saudi Aramco and aviation, saying facilities are “within range” and warning airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
- The conflict has intensified since July, with attacks killing 24 in Saudi Arabia and an airport strike in Riyadh killing at least 13.
- The war has displaced more than 300,000 people in western Yemen, while the UN says more than 1,600 have been killed since fighting restarted.
AI generated
SANAA – Houthi media, citing an anonymous military official, on Nov 1 repeated threats against Saudi oil giant Aramco and aviation in the kingdom.
Yemen’s Houthis, fighting a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government, are allies of Iran, which on Nov 1 warned the US and Israel not to renew strikes on the Islamic republic after they had threatened a return to war.
“Aramco facilities are within range of the Yemeni Armed Forces, and investments in them are a venture fraught with losses,” the Houthis’ Saba news agency quoted the military official as saying.
The official also warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace “except for the airspaces of Mecca and Medina”.
The Houthis have targeted oil facilities and airports in the kingdom since Yemen’s once-dormant war reignited in July, killing 24 people in Saudi Arabia in October.
An Oct 10 strike on Riyadh’s international airport became the deadliest on Saudi soil in years when it killed at least 13 people.
On Nov 1, the coalition said it had intercepted a missile and a drone both launched by the Houthis “towards the southern region”.
Meanwhile, fighting in Yemen has displaced more than 300,000 people in the western part of the impoverished country.
Most of them forced from their homes in the last two months, the displaced “urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care”, the International Organization for Migration said in a statement on Nov 1.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed since fighting in Yemen reignited.
Saba on Nov 1 said that Saudi Arabia had “targeted the Faculty of Medicine at Hodeidah University with two raids”, and two Hodeidah residents told AFP they heard an explosion in the area.
The coalition, for its part, said on Nov 1 it had conducted “a precision operation to neutralise vital resources” used by the Houthis, and published video footage that it said showed attacks on the Hodeideh and Dhamar governorates.
A fragile 2022 truce fell apart in July after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks. AFP

A456.text:
Longest truce of Ukraine war ends in Kherson
KYIV – The longest truce of the Ukraine war, limited to the eastern Kherson region, ended on Nov 1 after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.
The rare pause in fighting, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and which began early on Oct 27, enabled a humanitarian mission to go into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as the war grinds through its fifth year.
Neither side reported violations after the truce began, in what one Ukrainian lawmaker described as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”.
“The ceasefire, which was in effect from Oct 27 to Nov 1, has ended,” said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights.
He called the temporary truce “an important step in our joint humanitarian efforts” with Russia.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume in November, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
On Nov 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries – as US counterpart Donald Trump had demanded – if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.
Raid alert app hack
Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin warned residents to be particularly vigilant when the ceasefire ended and to “respond immediately to warnings about Russian attacks”.
Later on Nov 1, Ukraine’s air force and anti-disinformation centre said it suspected the country’s air raid alert system had been hacked, after false alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the application.
The announcement came minutes after the end of the truce.
“The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference,” the force said in a message. “There is no radiation threat.”
Air force spokesman Yuriy Ignat confirmed to AFP that the app had been hacked.
SPRAVDI, Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications, blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
A separate app, which deals specifically with the Ukrainian capital, is still working normally, the Kyiv city authorities said.
Braced for ‘worse’
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022, the conflict has destroyed parts of eastern and southern Ukraine, left hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians dead, and forced millions to flee their homes.
AFP spoke to several Kherson residents, one of whom said the ceasefire had been a “breath of fresh air”.
“We have to use this time to get things done,” said Volodymyr Omeltchenko, a 38-year-old gardener. “We’re pruning the rose bushes for winter.”
Pope Leo, who had pressed Russia for a truce in Oleshky, said he hoped the temporary pause would “strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives”.
A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern that the fighting would be “worse than before” when it resumed.
Russian forces, positioned on the other side of the Dnipro river, had taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks, and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions using surveillance drones, the officer said.
Refinery reportedly hit
Both Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes elsewhere on Nov 1.
Russia said early on Nov 1 that a drone had struck an “industrial enterprise” east of Moscow overnight.
Ukrainian media reported that Kyiv had attacked the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it “one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants”.
Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites, in what it says is fair retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump had been pressing Kyiv to stop such attacks, blaming them for rising diesel costs that analysts attribute to the Iran war.
On Nov 1, Zelensky referred to conversations he had had with Trump and his team on the issue, in an interview with Fox News.

A457.text:
UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years, UN chief says
The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in the Western Sahara region will come to an end after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said on Nov 1.
Morocco, which claims the Western Sahara as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.
The Polisario Front has been seeking an independent state in Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain left in 1976.
A peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place there since a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991.
November 1 would mark the start of the “liquidation phase” of the mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement.
The end of the peacekeeping mission comes a year after the UN Security Council adopted a US-drafted resolution that accepted Rabat’s plan to give the territory autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most feasible” solution to the conflict.
Russia, which abstained in last year’s vote, this year vetoed another US-backed resolution that would have cemented the UN’s preference for the Moroccan plan while scaling back the peacekeeping force.
The Security Council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
Besides monitoring the ceasefire, MINURSO was tasked with organising a referendum that has never taken place due to disagreements over voter eligibility.
Morocco’s Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita told state media that the mission’s reference to a referendum - the “R” in its name - was an “anachronism”.
Rabat had been informed that Russia was going to block the US-drafted resolution, but saw it as “an opportunity to review certain rules of the game”, he said.
Morocco’s royal palace had said the non-renewal of the mission was a “significant development” towards withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council.
Algeria’s Foreign Ministry on Oct 31 expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario said in a statement it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”. REUTERS

A464.text:
France launches ‘attempted murder’ probe after petrol bomb attack on security forces
- France has opened an attempted murder probe after petrol bombs hit security forces during Paris protests against rising living costs.
- Prosecutors said around 15 gendarmes and police were targeted; one officer suffered burns, and no suspect has been arrested.
- More than 770 people were arrested nationwide, while shop damage was lower than before, though retailers fear harm before the holiday season.
AI generated
PARIS – France has launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris, prosecutors told AFP on Nov 1.
On Oct 31, clashes erupted in the capital and some other cities after hundreds of thousands of people staged a third weekend of protests against soaring living costs.
The Paris police prefecture said that several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has decried an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters.
“Explosive devices were thrown at around 15 gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Nov 1.
Gendarmes are military police officers who are part of the French armed forces.
Prosecutors said an investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Dramatic images, including AFP photos and video, showed a homemade incendiary device exploding at the feet of a security officer in eastern Paris, engulfing his lower body in flames.
An assessment of the injured was ongoing, prosecutors said, adding that the reported injuries include second-degree burns.
Initial complaints were expected to be filed on Nov 1.
The gendarme struck by the Molotov cocktail told French television of the burns he suffered, describing “skin that stings” and a “rain” of projectiles thrown at his unit.
Fewer shops damaged
The gendarmerie said that 13 members of the officer’s unit were injured, according to RTL.
No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident”, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.
The protests come in a tense political climate, with presidential elections six months away and front runner Marine le Pen vowing to restore law and order if elected in 2027.
The leader of the far-right National Rally party said those responsible for the firebomb attack must be “punished with the utmost severity”, in a post on X.
Both she and Bruno Retailleau, head of the right-wing Republicans, described images of the officer in flames as “unbearable”.
The right-leaning Le Figaro said: “The days of the May 1968 riots are a far cry from today, when gendarmes facing the most violent protesters wore... ties.”
More than 770 people were arrested during weekend protests in France, the Interior Ministry said on Nov 1. It added that there had been “no major incidents” late on Oct 31.
A total of 159 members of law enforcement were injured during protests and Halloween celebrations, it said.
The number of shops damaged on the sidelines of the Oct 31 protests was significantly lower than during previous weekends, with some 20 businesses affected, according to France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
But CCI France voiced concern about the impact of the protests on retail activity ahead of the year-end holiday season, a peak period for businesses. AFP

A516.text:
French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living have shaken a number of countries this autumn.
Violence erupted in the French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.
As the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.
In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.
The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged in one of the worst nights of urban unrest in France’s recent history.
In Germany, looters and rioters rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.
“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”
Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of violence like those in Paris were prevented thanks to our highly committed police forces,” he said.
More than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.
Hooded rioters damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.
More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.
Most of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.
Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.
In Portugal, riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.
The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a bill that makes evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.
In Albania, masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.

A521.text:
More than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027, with the Bank of England expected to begin raising interest rates this week.
The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) is widely expected to increase the base rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November after UK inflation rose further to 3.5% in September.
It could be the first of four quarter-point rises over the next 12 months, according to financial market expectations, which would exacerbate the financial pressure on households grappling with higher energy and food bills.
Thousands of borrowers are due to come off fixed contracts in the final months of this year, with 700,000 having been forecast to switch over to new rates between July and December.
A further 2.3m households will reach the end of their fixed rates next year, according to data collected by UK Finance, a banking industry body.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets – triggered in part by energy prices and inflation fears linked to the war in the Middle East – has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
An increase in the Bank of England rate could drive those rates, and wider household costs, even higher.
Data released last week showed that mortgage approvals in the UK fell to a near three-year low in September as potential buyers were deterred by the jump in borrowing costs.
Alongside last week’s budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) warned that household disposable incomes would fall by 0.6% next year after taking account of inflation. The downgrade compares with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes the watchdog had forecast in March – an outlook the OBR’s David Miles described as “a pretty grim picture”.
That income squeeze is also being driven by the energy price shock, which the OBR said would push consumer inflation to 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.
Ofgem’s energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to rise by more than £400 in January, according to the latest forecast from EDF.
John Healey, the chancellor, made a £100 payout to 20m households the centrepiece of his budget, saying he wanted to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”.
His cost of living package – which also included cancelling fuel duty rises planned by Rachel Reeves and extending a VAT cut on electricity bills – was paid for by tax rises on banks, savers and landlords.
The Bank of England has taken a wait-and-see approach to rising inflation since the start of the Iran war, in contrast to other central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, which have already raised borrowing costs this year.
Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, has made clear that the MPC is watching closely to see if rising prices are being passed through into higher wages for workers – evidence of the so-called “second-round effects” that can lead to inflation becoming embedded.
Before the war in the Middle East, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates several times this year, with inflation expected to drift back down towards its 2% target.
But an extended period of historically high oil prices, affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz choking off supplies, has instead fed through into high and rising inflation.
The Bank will publish updated forecasts for economic growth and inflation alongside its interest rate decision this week.
The UK economy beat expectations to be the joint fastest-growing in the G7 in the first half of 2026, which the Office for National Statistics said was partly driven by AI-related sectors.
But official forecasts for next year have been cut sharply amid fears that the higher cost of energy will eventually start to weigh on economic growth.

A553.text:
The FBI says North Korea was behind the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist that hit Binance on October 29th. The FBI labeled the activity “TraderTraitor” and said that it had observed actors it has connected to hack converting the tokens to Ethereum and preparing for further laundering of the funds. The agency offered few other details or evidence. The statement says:
North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
The FBI says that malicious actors from North Korea stole $6.3 billion worth of Crypto from Binance customers.
North Korea Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor.”
The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.
As expected, Binance reopened customer withdrawals today after freezing them in the immediate aftermath of the hack.
